opus-5.5.text:
I think the clearest signal is when you have a task that's really specific to your domain or your business, something the base model just isn't going to have seen much of in pretraining, and where you've already pushed prompting as far as it can go. A lot of people jump to fine-tuning too early. My first advice is always: try really hard with prompt engineering, give good examples, break the task down. If you hit a ceiling there and the task is genuinely important to you, that's when reinforcement fine-tuning starts to make sense.

The other big thing is whether you can grade the output. Reinforcement fine-tuning works best when you can tell whether an answer is good, ideally in a fairly objective way. Things like legal or medical reasoning where an expert can say "this is correct," classifying something into a known set of categories, or extracting the right information from a document. If you can write a grader that reliably scores the model's attempts, you can get a lot out of surprisingly few examples, sometimes dozens or hundreds rather than the huge datasets you'd need for supervised fine-tuning.

So I'd frame it as three questions. Is this task high-value enough to justify the investment? Have you actually exhausted what you can do with prompting and the off-the-shelf model? And can you define what "good" looks like clearly enough to grade it? If the answer to all three is yes, it's probably worth trying.

One more thing: the eval work you do to answer that third question pays off regardless. Even if you never end up fine-tuning, having a really good way to measure performance on your task makes it much easier to evaluate each new model as it comes out. Sometimes the next base model just solves your problem.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is: later than most people assume. The first thing I'd always push someone toward is prompting and just getting the base model to do as much as it can. The models are really good now, and a lot of what looks like a capability gap is actually a specification gap. You haven't told the model clearly enough what you want, or you haven't given it the right tools or the right context. So I'd exhaust that first, and I'd build a really good eval while I'm doing it, because you need that regardless.

Where reinforcement fine-tuning starts to make sense is when you have a task where you can reliably tell whether the model got it right, but the model still isn't getting there with prompting. It's that combination that matters. You need a grader. It could be a verifiable answer, like a correct code output or a correct classification against expert labels, or it could be a rubric that a model can apply consistently. If you can't grade it, you can't do RL well, and you'll just end up reinforcing noise.

The other signal is that the task is narrow and the domain is deep. The places I've seen it work best are things like a specialized medical or legal classification task, or a very particular kind of code transformation, where there's real expertise encoded in what "correct" means and the general model only has a partial sense of it. You don't need a huge amount of data for that. Dozens to a few hundred really high-quality examples can move things a lot, which is very different from supervised fine-tuning, where you're trying to show the model the exact output you want on every example.

And then I'd think about the economics. If you're running something at very high volume and a smaller RL-tuned model can match or beat a frontier model with a long prompt, that's a real win on latency and cost. If it's a task you run a few hundred times a day, it's probably not worth the investment, because every time the base models improve you're going to want to redo it.

So the short version: start with prompting and evals, make sure you have a grader you trust, and reach for RFT when the task is narrow, well-defined, and important enough that the gap between the prompted model and what you need is actually costing you something.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking: can you reliably grade the output? Reinforcement fine-tuning is a good fit when you have a specific task where the model’s answers can vary in quality, and you can give it a useful signal about which answers are better.

Before investing in that, I’d establish a baseline with prompting and a solid evaluation set. If the model already does well enough, you may not need fine-tuning. But if there’s a persistent gap on a task that matters to your business, and you can measure that gap, then it’s worth exploring.

The grader is really central. It doesn’t have to mean there’s one exact correct answer, but it does have to capture what you actually care about. Otherwise, you can end up training the model to get a higher score without making it more useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking whether you can reliably grade the result. Reinforcement fine-tuning is a good fit when you have a specific task where the model is getting some answers right, but you want it to be much more consistent, and you can give it a meaningful reward signal for doing well.

I’d try prompting first, make sure the model has the information and tools it needs, and build an evaluation set. If you’re still seeing a gap, and closing that gap is valuable enough for your business, then it makes sense to invest in fine-tuning. The key is having a grader that actually captures what you care about. Otherwise, you can end up training the model to get a higher score without making it more useful.
